vignette:
He is 54, married, and has spent much of his adult life in the air, where he has always trusted training, instinct, and repetition to keep him safe. As a combat pilot, he has lived for years with high stakes and tight control, and he describes that control as part of what made the job tolerable. The accident that changed him happens during a routine operational flight that turns catastrophic without warning. In his telling, there is no dramatic buildup, only a sudden mechanical failure, a violent loss of stability, and the immediate knowledge that he may not make it back. He remembers the cockpit filling with alarms, the body tightening before thought can catch up, and the strange narrowing of time as he fights through emergency procedures while the aircraft becomes harder to manage by the second.

He survives, but the survival does not feel clean or complete. In the days afterward, while colleagues speak to him with relief and pride, he feels detached from their responses, as if they are discussing someone else’s event. He is physically shaken, sleeping poorly, jolting awake at the smallest noise, and replaying the sequence again and again in his mind, searching for the moment he might have done something differently. He begins to notice how often he returns to the same details: the pitch of the warning tone, the smell in the cockpit, the feel of the controls fighting him. These images come uninvited, most strongly when he is trying to rest or when he is alone and not actively occupied.

At home, his wife sees that he is not the same man who left for work before the accident. He becomes quieter, less patient, and more easily startled by ordinary things like a slammed door or a sudden ringtone. He does not like to describe what happened, but he also does not like when no one asks, because silence leaves him alone with it. He starts to avoid conversation about flying, especially anything that resembles analysis or debriefing. Even though his profession requires him to think clearly about risk, he finds himself steering away from aviation news, hangars, and stories from former colleagues. He feels shame about this, because he has always seen himself as resilient and disciplined. Now, he experiences his own body as unreliable, his nerves apparently too close to the surface.

Returning to work is not simple. He goes back because that is what he expects of himself, and because part of him still wants the structure of the cockpit. Yet once he is near aircraft again, his body reacts before his mind can reassure it. He scans for danger more intensely than before, and he notices every sound, every vibration, every change in equipment with an alertness that borders on exhaustion. The vigilance is useful in the moment but costly afterward; by the end of a shift, he feels worn down, irritable, and unable to relax. He begins to sleep in fragments, waking several times a night, sometimes with his heart pounding and the sense that he is still in the accident. On some nights he lies awake waiting for morning, counting the hours, then feeling resentful and tired when the day begins.

Over time, he also notices a kind of narrowing in his emotional life. Things that used to matter in ordinary ways now feel distant. He still cares for his wife and family, but he is less spontaneous with them, less inclined to laughter, less able to stay present when they talk about future plans. He goes through the motions of meals, errands, and work obligations, yet often feels as if part of him remains back in that damaged aircraft, still trying to bring it under control. He is bothered by a persistent sense of vulnerability, especially in moments when he would once have felt competent. He does not trust calm when it arrives, because he has learned how quickly calm can be broken.

In sessions, he speaks with the measured language of someone used to keeping himself contained, but there are moments when the strain shows in the pauses between sentences. He describes feeling on edge much of the time, as though his body is waiting for another emergency. He is aware that the accident has changed the way he moves through the world: he checks exits, he anticipates worst-case scenarios, and he has little tolerance for surprises. Even now, months later, the event is not over for him. It returns in flashes, in dreams, in his body’s sudden alarm, and in the quiet moments when he is trying hardest to appear fine.
